topics.title: System, surroundings, state variables and state functions

learn.hook: A pressure cooker on your stove, a sealed tiffin and a vacuum flask of chai are the three textbook systems of thermodynamics, sitting in an Indian kitchen.
points: The system is the part of the universe we study; everything else is the surroundings. System + surroundings = universe. The boundary may be real or imaginary.

Open system: exchanges both energy and matter with the surroundings (an open beaker of reactants). Closed system: exchanges energy but not matter (a closed steel vessel). Isolated system: exchanges neither (reactants in a perfectly insulated thermos flask).
The state of a system is described by measurable macroscopic properties called state variables: pressure (p), volume (V), temperature (T) and amount (n). Fixing a few of them fixes the state.

A state function depends only on the initial and final states, not on how the change happened: U, H, S, G, p, V, T. Climbing from Mumbai to Lonavala gives the same change in height whatever road you take.
A path function depends on the route taken: heat (q) and work (w). Their values change if the same initial and final states are connected differently.

example.q: Classify: (i) tea in an open cup, (ii) coffee in a sealed steel bottle, (iii) soup in a perfectly insulated, sealed thermos.
steps: Open cup: steam escapes (matter) and heat is lost (energy) → open system.
Sealed steel bottle: no matter leaves, but heat flows through steel → closed system.
Ideal sealed thermos: neither heat nor matter crosses → isolated system.

learn.reallife: Cold-chain boxes that carried vaccines to remote villages during India's immunisation drives are designed to behave as nearly isolated systems for many hours.

topics.title: Internal energy, heat, work and the first law

learn.hook: Energy is like money in a UPI wallet: it can come in as heat or as work, go out either way, but the balance only changes by exactly what flows in and out.
points: Internal energy (U) is the total energy of a system: chemical, electrical, mechanical and other forms. It is a state function; we can measure only its change, ΔU.
Adiabatic process: no heat transfer between system and surroundings (insulated walls). Then ΔU = w_ad, the adiabatic work, which depends only on initial and final states (Joule's experiments).
Heat transfer through conducting walls also changes U: if no work is done, ΔU = q.
IUPAC sign convention: q is positive when heat is absorbed by the system and negative when released; w is positive when work is done on the system and negative when work is done by the system.
First law of thermodynamics: energy of an isolated system is constant; energy can be neither created nor destroyed. In general, ΔU = q + w.

example.q: A system absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on the surroundings. Find ΔU.
steps: Work done by the system: w = −200 J

learn.reallife: In an Indian Railways diesel locomotive, fuel's internal energy becomes heat in the cylinders and work on the pistons. The first law tracks every joule: heat absorbed by the gas minus work it does equals its change in internal energy.

options: Entropy of the universe always increases

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Adiabatic: ΔU = w > 0, and higher internal energy of an ideal gas shows up as higher temperature, as when a bicycle pump warms up.
quiz.mistake: Thinks compression without heat cannot change temperature

teach.ask: Gappu's gas absorbed 500 J and did 200 J of work. 'What happened to its internal energy? What are the sign rules?'
teach.praise: Wonderful! ΔU = q + w with heat absorbed and work done on the system positive, so ΔU = +300 J. Gappu's energy books are balanced!
teach.nudge: Close! What equation is the first law, and which signs do q and w take when heat is absorbed and work is done by the gas?

topics.title: Pressure–volume work and reversible isothermal expansion

learn.hook: Steam pushing a piston moved the first trains in India in 1853. That push is pressure–volume work, and how slowly you let the gas expand decides how much work you get.
points: Work of expansion against a constant external pressure: w = −p_ex ΔV = −p_ex (V_f − V_i). Expansion (ΔV > 0) gives negative w (work done by the system); compression gives positive w.

A reversible process is carried out infinitely slowly through a series of equilibrium states, so the external pressure differs from the internal pressure only by an infinitesimal amount. It can be reversed at any instant by an infinitesimal change.
Reversible work is the maximum work a system can do on expansion (or the minimum work needed for compression), because p_ex always nearly equals the gas pressure.
For reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas: w_rev = −2.303 nRT log(V_f/V_i) = −2.303 nRT log(p_i/p_f).
Free expansion: expansion into vacuum (p_ex = 0) does no work, w = 0, whether reversible or not.

example.q: 1 mol of an ideal gas at 300 K expands reversibly and isothermally from 1 L to 10 L. Find w (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹).
example.answer: w ≈ −5.74 kJ (work done by the gas)

learn.reallife: Steam turbines at NTPC power stations let steam expand through many stages instead of one sudden blast. Expanding the gas more gradually gets more useful work out of it, a practical echo of reversible work.

Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Free, irreversible and reversible routes between the same states give different work, so work depends on path.
quiz.mistake: Thinks work depends only on the initial and final volumes

teach.ask: Gappu expands a gas from 2 L to 10 L against 1 atm. 'How much work? And why do reversible expansions give more work?'
teach.praise: Superb! w = −p_ex ΔV = −8 L atm, and a slow reversible path keeps p_ex nearly equal to the gas pressure, giving maximum work. Gappu's piston is happy!
teach.nudge: Good! Which pressure goes into w = −p_ex ΔV, what is its sign for expansion, and why does a reversible path give the most work?

topics.title: q, w and ΔU for isothermal and free expansion

learn.hook: Let a gas expand at constant temperature and its internal energy does not budge, yet heat flows in and work flows out. The first law makes these two cancel exactly.
points: For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature. In any isothermal process (T constant), ΔU = 0, so q = −w.
Isothermal irreversible expansion against constant p_ex: w = −p_ex(V_f − V_i) and q = −w = p_ex(V_f − V_i).
Isothermal reversible expansion: w = −2.303 nRT log(V_f/V_i) and q = +2.303 nRT log(V_f/V_i).
Free expansion into vacuum: w = 0; for an ideal gas q = 0 and ΔU = 0 as well (no intermolecular forces to overcome).
Adiabatic change: q = 0, so ΔU = w. For compression ΔU > 0 and the gas warms; for expansion ΔU < 0 and the gas cools.

example.q: 3 L of an ideal gas at 6 atm expands isothermally to 9 L (a) into vacuum, (b) against a constant external pressure of 2 atm. Find q, w and ΔU for each.
steps: Isothermal ideal gas → ΔU = 0 in both cases.
example.answer: (a) q = w = ΔU = 0; (b) w = −12 L atm, q = +12 L atm, ΔU = 0

learn.reallife: LPG cylinders feel cold when gas is released quickly: the expanding gas does work and, with little time for heat to flow in, it cools. If you release it slowly, heat from the surroundings keeps it nearly isothermal.

topics.title: Enthalpy and the relation ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT

learn.hook: Most reactions in your kitchen, your body and in Indian industry happen in open air at roughly constant pressure. Enthalpy is the energy bookkeeping designed for exactly that situation.
points: Enthalpy H = U + pV. It is a state function.
At constant pressure, the heat absorbed equals the enthalpy change: ΔH = q_p. At constant volume, ΔU = q_v. Negative ΔH means an exothermic reaction; positive ΔH means endothermic.
For reactions involving gases (ideal behaviour, constant T and p): ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT, where Δn_g = moles of gaseous products − moles of gaseous reactants.
If Δn_g = 0 (e.g. C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), or H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g)), then ΔH = ΔU. Solids and liquids are ignored when counting Δn_g because their volume changes are negligible.
Use R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, and keep units consistent: convert J to kJ (divide by 1000) before adding to ΔU in kJ.

example.q: The enthalpy of vaporisation of water at 373 K is 40.79 kJ mol⁻¹. Find ΔU for H₂O(l) → H₂O(g), treating the vapour as ideal.

learn.reallife: In a pressure cooker the steam is trapped (nearly constant volume), while an open pan boils at constant pressure. That is why chemists distinguish ΔU (bomb calorimeters) from ΔH (open beakers).

quiz.q: For which reaction is ΔH equal to ΔU?
quiz.explain: Δn_g = 2 − 2 = 0, so Δn_g RT = 0 and ΔH = ΔU.
quiz.mistake: Counts solids or liquids when finding Δn_g

quiz.q: ΔH for combustion of methane, CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), is −890.3 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K. What is ΔU in kJ mol⁻¹ (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)?

quiz.q: At constant pressure, the heat absorbed by a system equals:

quiz.q: The enthalpy of vaporisation of water at 373 K is 40.79 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔU of vaporisation in kJ mol⁻¹ (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Adds Δn_g RT instead of subtracting

quiz.q: What is Δn_g for 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g)?
quiz.explain: Gaseous products 2 − gaseous reactants 3 = −1.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts in the wrong order (reactants − products)

quiz.q: A reaction has ΔH = −50 kJ. Which statement is correct?

It is exothermic: heat is released at constant pressure
quiz.explain: Negative ΔH means the system releases heat to the surroundings.
quiz.mistake: Reads the negative sign as 'absorbed'

quiz.q: For the decomposition CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g) at 1000 K, by how much does ΔH exceed ΔU, in kJ mol⁻¹ (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)?

quiz.q: Assertion (A): For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), ΔH is more negative than ΔU. Reason (R): Δn_g for this reaction is negative.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Δn_g = −2, so ΔH = ΔU − 2RT, making ΔH more negative than ΔU.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is enthalpy, and how do I get ΔU if I know ΔH for a gas reaction?'
teach.praise: Fantastic! H = U + pV, ΔH is the heat at constant pressure, and ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT using gaseous moles only. Gappu converts like a pro!
teach.nudge: Good! What is H in terms of U, and how do gaseous moles enter the link between ΔH and ΔU?

topics.title: Extensive and intensive properties; heat capacity

learn.hook: A full matka and a small glass of water from it are at the same temperature, but the matka needs far more heat to warm up. That difference is extensive versus intensive.
points: Extensive properties depend on the amount of matter: mass, volume, internal energy, enthalpy, heat capacity. Intensive properties do not: temperature, pressure, density, molar volume, specific heat, molar heat capacity.
The ratio of two extensive properties is intensive: density = mass/volume; molar volume = V/n.

Heat capacity C: heat needed to raise the temperature of a body by 1 K; q = C ΔT. Specific heat capacity c: per gram (J g⁻¹ K⁻¹), so q = c × m × ΔT. Molar heat capacity C_m: per mole (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹), q = n C_m ΔT. Water: c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.
C_p (constant pressure) is larger than C_v (constant volume), because at constant pressure some heat also goes into work of expansion.
For an ideal gas: C_p − C_v = R (per mole), with R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

example.q: How much heat is needed to warm 250 g of water from 25 °C to 75 °C (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹)?
steps: ΔT = 75 − 25 = 50 K (a change of 50 °C equals 50 K)

learn.reallife: Water's high specific heat is why coastal cities like Chennai and Mumbai have milder temperature swings than Delhi: the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal absorb and release huge amounts of heat with little temperature change.

teach.praise: Excellent! Temperature is intensive, heat capacity is extensive, and specific heat is per gram. Gappu warms his matka with confidence!
teach.nudge: Nice! Does temperature change if you take half the sample? And how is specific heat different from heat capacity?

learn.hook: The calorie count printed on a biscuit packet comes from burning the food in a steel bomb surrounded by water and measuring how hot the water gets.
points: A calorimeter measures heat from the temperature change of a known heat sink: q = C_cal × ΔT, where C_cal is the heat capacity of the calorimeter and its contents.
Bomb calorimeter: a strong sealed steel vessel (the bomb) immersed in water. The sample burns in excess oxygen at constant volume, so no work is done and the heat measured is q_v = ΔU.
Constant-pressure (coffee-cup) calorimeter: an insulated container open to the atmosphere. Heat measured is q_p = ΔH, used for reactions in solution such as neutralisation.
Sign: heat released by the reaction is absorbed by the calorimeter, so q_reaction = −C_cal ΔT. A rise in temperature means an exothermic reaction (negative ΔU or ΔH).
Lab safety: wear goggles; handle acids and alkalis carefully; never seal and heat an ordinary container; bomb calorimeters are filled with oxygen only under supervision, behind a safety screen.

example.q: 1.20 g of graphite is burnt in a bomb calorimeter in excess O₂. The temperature rises by 1.60 K. The calorimeter's heat capacity is 24.5 kJ K⁻¹. Find ΔU per mole of carbon (C = 12 g mol⁻¹).
steps: ΔU = −39.2 ÷ 0.100 = −392 kJ mol⁻¹ (at constant volume, heat = ΔU)

learn.reallife: FSSAI-approved food labs in India use bomb calorimeters to check the energy values (kcal) printed on packaged snacks, biscuits and energy drinks.

quiz.q: 50 mL of 1.0 M HCl and 50 mL of 1.0 M NaOH are mixed in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The temperature rises by 6.8 K. Taking mass of solution 100 g and c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, what is ΔH of neutralisation in kJ per mole of water formed?
quiz.mistake: Uses 0.1 mol (adding both reactants) or forgets the negative sign

quiz.q: Why is the heat measured in a coffee-cup calorimeter equal to ΔH?
options: The reaction occurs at constant (atmospheric) pressure
The reaction occurs at constant volume
quiz.explain: Heat exchanged at constant pressure is q_p = ΔH.
quiz.mistake: Thinks open calorimeters measure ΔU

quiz.q: In a calorimeter experiment the water temperature falls. What does this indicate about the reaction?
quiz.explain: The reaction absorbed heat from the water, so ΔH (or ΔU) is positive.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the link between temperature change and sign

quiz.q: 2 g of a fuel burns in a bomb calorimeter of heat capacity 15 kJ K⁻¹; the temperature rises by 4 K. What is the heat released per gram, in kJ g⁻¹?
quiz.explain: Total q = 15 × 4 = 60 kJ for 2 g, so 30 kJ g⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by the mass of fuel

quiz.q: Why must a bomb calorimeter be made of strong steel?
options: Combustion in pure oxygen at constant volume produces high pressure
quiz.explain: The sealed vessel must withstand the pressure generated by rapid combustion, which is also why it is used only with proper safety precautions.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the steel is part of the reaction

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Heat measured in a bomb calorimeter for a reaction involving gases may differ from its ΔH. Reason (R): A bomb calorimeter measures ΔU, and ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: When Δn_g ≠ 0, ΔH and ΔU differ by Δn_g RT, so the bomb value must be corrected to get ΔH.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ΔH and ΔU are always identical

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do chemists measure heat of combustion, and why do they get ΔU, not ΔH, from a bomb calorimeter?'
teach.praise: Superb! The sealed bomb keeps volume constant so q_v = ΔU, measured from q = C ΔT, while open calorimeters at constant pressure give ΔH. Gappu reads food labels differently now!
teach.nudge: Good! Is the volume or the pressure fixed in a bomb calorimeter, and how is heat found from the temperature change?

topics.title: Reaction enthalpy, standard states, phase changes and thermochemical equations

learn.hook: Sweating cools you because each mole of water that evaporates from your skin carries away more than 40 kJ of heat. Phase changes are enthalpy changes too.
points: Reaction enthalpy: Δ_rH = Σ(enthalpies of products) − Σ(enthalpies of reactants), each multiplied by its stoichiometric coefficient.
Standard enthalpy of reaction Δ_rH°: all substances in their standard states, i.e. the pure substance at 1 bar and a specified temperature (usually 298 K).

Phase transformations: enthalpy of fusion Δ_fusH° (solid → liquid; water 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹ at 273 K), enthalpy of vaporisation Δ_vapH° (liquid → gas; water 40.79 kJ mol⁻¹ at 373 K) and enthalpy of sublimation Δ_subH° (solid → gas) = Δ_fusH° + Δ_vapH° at the same temperature.
A thermochemical equation is a balanced equation with physical states and the Δ_rH value: C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l); Δ_cH° = −1367 kJ mol⁻¹.

Conventions: coefficients are moles; Δ_rH is per mole of reaction as written. Multiplying the equation by n multiplies Δ_rH by n; reversing the equation changes the sign of Δ_rH. States must be written because they change the value.

example.q: Given H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l), Δ_rH° = −285.8 kJ mol⁻¹, write Δ_rH° for 2H₂O(l) → 2H₂(g) + O₂(g).
steps: Reverse the equation: sign changes to +285.8 kJ mol⁻¹.

learn.reallife: Traditional earthen matkas cool water in Indian summers: water seeping through the pores evaporates, absorbing its enthalpy of vaporisation from the water inside.

games.title: Manipulate Δ_rH (given A → B, Δ_rH = −100 kJ mol⁻¹)

items.q: Δ_subH if Δ_fusH = 6 and Δ_vapH = 45 (kJ mol⁻¹)

quiz.q: What does the standard state of a substance mean?
options: The substance at 1 atm and 0 °C only
The pure substance at 1 bar and a specified temperature
quiz.explain: Standard state refers to the pure form at 1 bar; the temperature is specified, usually 298 K.
quiz.mistake: Confuses standard state with STP

quiz.q: Δ_fusH of ice is 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹ and Δ_vapH of water is 45.07 kJ mol⁻¹ at 273 K. What is Δ_subH of ice at 273 K in kJ mol⁻¹?
quiz.explain: Δ_subH = Δ_fusH + Δ_vapH = 6.01 + 45.07 = 51.08 kJ mol⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts instead of adding

quiz.q: For 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l), Δ_rH° = −571.6 kJ mol⁻¹. What is Δ_rH° for H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l) in kJ mol⁻¹?
quiz.explain: Halving the equation halves Δ_rH: −571.6/2 = −285.8.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the same value after changing coefficients

quiz.q: Why must physical states be written in a thermochemical equation?
options: The enthalpy change depends on the states of reactants and products
quiz.explain: Forming H₂O(l) releases more heat than forming H₂O(g), because condensation releases extra enthalpy.
quiz.mistake: Thinks state symbols are decoration

quiz.q: How much heat in kJ is needed to melt 36 g of ice at 273 K (Δ_fusH = 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹, H₂O = 18 g mol⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by mass instead of moles

quiz.q: If the reaction A → B has Δ_rH = +40 kJ mol⁻¹, then for B → A, Δ_rH is:
quiz.explain: Reversing a reaction reverses the sign of its enthalpy change.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the sign the same on reversal

quiz.q: Which equation correctly expresses the standard reaction enthalpy?
options: Δ_rH° = Σ aᵢ H°(products) − Σ bᵢ H°(reactants)
quiz.explain: Products minus reactants, each weighted by its stoichiometric coefficient.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the order of subtraction

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Burning 2 mol of methane releases twice the heat of burning 1 mol. Reason (R): Enthalpy change is an extensive property.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: ΔH scales with the amount reacting; doubling the coefficients doubles ΔH.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ΔH is fixed regardless of amount

teach.ask: Gappu has ΔH for making 1 mol of water. 'What happens to ΔH if I reverse the reaction or double it? And what are fusion and vaporisation enthalpies?'
teach.praise: Superb! Reverse the reaction and flip the sign, multiply it and multiply ΔH, and phase changes have their own enthalpies. Gappu's thermochemistry is solid!
teach.nudge: Close! What happens to the sign on reversing, to the value on doubling, and which enthalpy goes with melting or boiling?

topics.title: Standard enthalpy of formation and Hess's law

learn.hook: You cannot burn carbon to only CO without some CO₂ forming, so nobody can measure ΔH for C → CO directly. Hess's law finds it anyway, with nothing but arithmetic.
points: Standard molar enthalpy of formation Δ_fH°: the enthalpy change when 1 mol of a compound is formed from its elements in their most stable states (reference states) at 1 bar. E.g. C(graphite) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), Δ_fH° = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹.
Δ_fH° of an element in its reference state is zero: C(graphite), O₂(g), H₂(g), N₂(g), Br₂(l), Na(s).
Δ_rH° = Σ a Δ_fH°(products) − Σ b Δ_fH°(reactants).

Hess's law of constant heat summation: if a reaction takes place in several steps, its standard enthalpy is the sum of the standard enthalpies of the steps, at the same temperature. It follows from H being a state function.
To use Hess's law, reverse and multiply the given equations so that, when added, they give the target equation; apply the same operations to their ΔH values.

example.q: Find Δ_rH° for C(graphite) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g), given (i) C(graphite) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH° = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹ and (ii) CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH° = −283.0 kJ mol⁻¹.
steps: Add: C + O₂ + CO₂ → CO₂ + CO + ½O₂; cancel to C + ½O₂ → CO

learn.reallife: Steel plants at Jamshedpur and Bhilai rely on carbon monoxide to reduce iron ore in blast furnaces. The heat budget for making CO is calculated with Hess's law.

games.title: Solving a Hess's law problem

quiz.q: Calculate Δ_cH° of methane: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), given Δ_fH° (kJ mol⁻¹): CH₄ = −74.8, CO₂ = −393.5, H₂O(l) = −285.8.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the coefficient 2 for water or subtracts in the wrong order

quiz.q: Which equation represents the standard enthalpy of formation of water?
quiz.explain: Formation means one mole of compound from elements in their reference states (H₂ and O₂ gases, not atoms).
quiz.mistake: Writes 2 mol of product or uses atoms instead of molecules

quiz.q: What is Δ_fH° of O₂(g) at 298 K?
quiz.explain: O₂(g) is the reference state of oxygen, so its standard enthalpy of formation is zero.
quiz.mistake: Confuses O₂ with O₃ or O atoms

quiz.q: Given S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g), ΔH = −297 kJ and 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g), ΔH = −198 kJ, find ΔH for S(s) + 3/2 O₂(g) → SO₃(g), in kJ.
quiz.explain: Take the first equation as is (−297) and half the second (−99): −297 + (−99) = −396 kJ.
quiz.mistake: Adds the second equation without halving it

quiz.q: Hess's law is a consequence of the fact that:
quiz.explain: Since ΔH depends only on initial and final states, any route gives the same total.
quiz.mistake: Links it to the second law instead of the state-function nature of H

quiz.q: Given Δ_fH° (kJ mol⁻¹): NH₃(g) = −46.1. What is Δ_rH° for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), in kJ mol⁻¹?
quiz.explain: 2 × (−46.1) − 0 = −92.2 kJ mol⁻¹, since N₂ and H₂ are elements in their reference states.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply by the coefficient 2

quiz.q: C(graphite) → C(diamond) has Δ_rH° = +1.9 kJ mol⁻¹. What is Δ_fH° of diamond in kJ mol⁻¹?
quiz.explain: Graphite is the reference state (Δ_fH° = 0), so Δ_fH°(diamond) = +1.9 kJ mol⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every form of an element has zero enthalpy of formation

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The enthalpy change for C → CO₂ is the same whether carbon burns directly or first to CO and then to CO₂. Reason (R): Hess's law says the total enthalpy change is independent of the path.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: −110.5 + (−283.0) = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹, the same as direct combustion.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a two-step route releases more heat

teach.ask: Gappu can't measure ΔH for C → CO directly. 'How can Hess's law help?'
teach.praise: Fantastic! Because H is a state function, you add up steps, flipping signs when you reverse and scaling when you multiply. Gappu found −110.5 kJ!
teach.nudge: Nearly! Why can enthalpies of steps be added, and what do you do to ΔH when you reverse or multiply an equation?

learn.hook: An LPG cylinder holds about 14.2 kg of mainly butane. Each mole burned releases about 2658 kJ, enough energy, cylinder by cylinder, to cook for a family for weeks.
points: Standard enthalpy of combustion Δ_cH°: enthalpy change per mole of a substance when it burns completely in oxygen, all substances in standard states. Butane: −2658.0 kJ mol⁻¹; glucose: −2802.0 kJ mol⁻¹. Combustion is always exothermic.

Enthalpy of atomisation Δ_aH°: enthalpy change to break one mole of bonds completely into gaseous atoms. H₂(g) → 2H(g): 435.0 kJ mol⁻¹; CH₄(g) → C(g) + 4H(g): 1665 kJ mol⁻¹; for metals it equals the enthalpy of sublimation, e.g. Na(s) → Na(g): 108.4 kJ mol⁻¹.

Bond dissociation enthalpy: for a diatomic molecule it equals the atomisation enthalpy (H–H 435.0 kJ mol⁻¹). In polyatomic molecules each successive bond needs a different energy, so we use mean bond enthalpy: C–H in CH₄ = 1665/4 = 416 kJ mol⁻¹.
For gas-phase reactions: Δ_rH° = Σ bond enthalpies of reactants (bonds broken) − Σ bond enthalpies of products (bonds formed).
Because mean values are used, bond-enthalpy estimates are approximate, unlike values from enthalpies of formation.

example.q: Estimate Δ_rH for H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g), using H–H = 435, Cl–Cl = 242 and H–Cl = 431 kJ mol⁻¹.

learn.reallife: Methane, the main component of the CNG that runs Delhi's buses, releases about 890 kJ per mole, roughly 55 MJ per kilogram. Engineers compare fuels like LPG, CNG and petrol by exactly this enthalpy of combustion per kilogram.

Energy to break 2 H–H bonds (435 each)
Mean O–H if atomisation of H₂O = 927

quiz.q: The enthalpy of atomisation of CH₄ is 1665 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the mean C–H bond enthalpy in kJ mol⁻¹?
quiz.explain: Four C–H bonds break: 1665/4 = 416.25 kJ mol⁻¹ (about 416).
quiz.mistake: Divides by the number of atoms (5) instead of bonds

quiz.q: Using bond enthalpies H–H = 436, Cl–Cl = 242 and H–Cl = 431 kJ mol⁻¹, estimate Δ_rH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl, in kJ.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts in the reverse order (formed − broken)

quiz.q: The standard enthalpy of combustion of glucose is −2802 kJ mol⁻¹. How much heat is released when 45 g of glucose (M = 180 g mol⁻¹) is burnt, in kJ?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by mass instead of moles

quiz.q: For a metal like sodium, the enthalpy of atomisation is the same as its:
quiz.explain: Na(s) → Na(g) gives separate gaseous atoms directly; this is sublimation.
quiz.mistake: Confuses atomisation with ionisation

quiz.q: Why are reaction enthalpies from mean bond enthalpies only approximate?
options: Mean bond enthalpies are averages over many compounds and do not match each molecule exactly
quiz.explain: A C–H bond in CH₄ is not identical to one in C₂H₆; averages introduce small errors.
quiz.mistake: Thinks bond enthalpies are exact for every molecule

quiz.q: Which bond-enthalpy expression is correct for a gas-phase reaction?
quiz.explain: Breaking bonds costs energy (positive); forming bonds releases it (negative).
quiz.mistake: Uses the products − reactants order from formation enthalpies

quiz.q: Using C–H = 414, Cl–Cl = 243, C–Cl = 330 and H–Cl = 431 kJ mol⁻¹, estimate Δ_rH for CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl, in kJ.
quiz.explain: Only one C–H and one Cl–Cl break (414 + 243 = 657); one C–Cl and one H–Cl form (330 + 431 = 761). Δ_rH = 657 − 761 = −104 kJ.
quiz.mistake: Counts all four C–H bonds as broken

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Combustion reactions are exothermic. Reason (R): In combustion, the bonds formed in CO₂ and H₂O are stronger overall than the bonds broken in the fuel and oxygen.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: More energy is released by forming strong C=O and O–H bonds than is needed to break C–H, C–C and O=O bonds.
quiz.mistake: Thinks heat comes from breaking bonds

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How can I estimate ΔH of a reaction from bond enthalpies?'
teach.praise: Excellent! ΔH = bonds broken − bonds formed; breaking costs energy, forming releases it. Gappu estimates like a chemical engineer!
teach.nudge: Good! Which bonds do you add first, which do you subtract, and why does breaking bonds need energy?

topics.title: Lattice enthalpy, Born–Haber cycle, solution and dilution enthalpies

learn.hook: Nobody can pull a crystal of salt apart into individual gaseous ions to measure it directly. Born and Haber built a closed loop of steps that measures it indirectly.
points: Lattice enthalpy Δ_latticeH°: enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic compound dissociates into its gaseous ions: NaCl(s) → Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g), +788 kJ mol⁻¹.

Born–Haber cycle for NaCl: Na(s) → Na(g) (sublimation, +108.4); Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻ (ionisation, +496); ½Cl₂(g) → Cl(g) (half bond dissociation, +121); Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g) (electron gain, −348.6); Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) → NaCl(s) (−lattice enthalpy). By Hess's law the sum equals Δ_fH°(NaCl) = −411.2 kJ mol⁻¹, giving Δ_latticeH° = +788 kJ mol⁻¹.

Enthalpy of solution Δ_solH°: enthalpy change when 1 mol of a substance dissolves in a specified amount of solvent. For ionic solids: Δ_solH° = Δ_latticeH° + Δ_hydH°. NaCl: 788 + (−784) = +4 kJ mol⁻¹, so it dissolves with slight cooling.
If lattice enthalpy is much larger than hydration enthalpy, the salt dissolves poorly or endothermically; large hydration enthalpies favour dissolution.

Enthalpy of dilution depends on how much solvent is added. Example: HCl(g) dissolving in 10, 25, 40 mol of water gives −69.01, −72.03, −72.79 kJ mol⁻¹, and at infinite dilution −74.85 kJ mol⁻¹, after which further dilution releases no heat.

example.q: Use the Born–Haber cycle data above to calculate the lattice enthalpy of NaCl.
steps: Δ_fH° = Δ_subH + Δ_iH + ½Δ_bondH + Δ_egH − Δ_latticeH

learn.reallife: Instant cold packs used by sports physios at cricket grounds contain ammonium nitrate, whose enthalpy of solution is positive. Dissolving it absorbs heat and chills the pack.

quiz.explain: Δ_solH = 700 + (−720) = −20 kJ mol⁻¹: it dissolves exothermically.

quiz.q: What does lattice enthalpy represent?

Energy to separate one mole of an ionic solid into gaseous ions
quiz.explain: It is defined for complete separation into gaseous ions, a positive quantity.
quiz.mistake: Confuses lattice enthalpy with melting or hydration

quiz.q: Which law makes the Born–Haber cycle possible?
quiz.explain: The sum of enthalpy changes round a closed cycle must equal the direct formation enthalpy.
quiz.mistake: Links the cycle to gas laws

quiz.q: HCl(g) in 10 mol H₂O: ΔH = −69.01 kJ mol⁻¹; in 40 mol H₂O: −72.79 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the enthalpy of dilution from 10 to 40 mol of water per mole of HCl, in kJ?
quiz.mistake: Adds the two values or reverses the subtraction

quiz.q: A salt has a lattice enthalpy much larger than the magnitude of its hydration enthalpy. It is expected to be:
options: Very soluble with release of heat
Poorly soluble, or soluble with absorption of heat
quiz.explain: If breaking the lattice costs far more than hydration returns, Δ_solH is strongly positive and dissolution is unfavourable.
quiz.mistake: Thinks high lattice enthalpy helps dissolution

quiz.q: In the Born–Haber cycle for NaCl, which step is exothermic?
quiz.explain: Chlorine releases 348.6 kJ mol⁻¹ when it gains an electron; the other three steps absorb energy.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ionisation releases energy

quiz.q: Assertion (A): NaCl dissolves in water although its lattice enthalpy is +788 kJ mol⁻¹. Reason (R): The hydration enthalpy of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ (−784 kJ mol⁻¹) almost balances the lattice enthalpy, and the entropy increase on dissolving helps.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Δ_solH is only +4 kJ mol⁻¹, and the increase in disorder when ions spread through water makes dissolution spontaneous.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only exothermic processes are spontaneous

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How did chemists get NaCl's lattice enthalpy if they can't measure it directly?'
teach.praise: Superb! The Born–Haber cycle uses Hess's law: sublimation, ionisation, dissociation, electron gain and formation enthalpies give 788 kJ mol⁻¹. Gappu is cycling happily!
teach.nudge: Close! Which law lets you add steps round a cycle, and which steps take Na(s) and Cl₂(g) to gaseous ions?

learn.hook: Ice melts on a Chennai afternoon even though melting absorbs heat. If 'releasing energy' were the only rule, that ice would never melt. Something else is pushing: disorder.
points: A spontaneous process takes place on its own, without continuous outside help, once started (it may still be slow). Examples: water flowing downhill, gas spreading into a vacuum, heat flowing from hot to cold. The reverse processes are non-spontaneous.

A decrease in enthalpy favours spontaneity, but it is not the only criterion: endothermic processes such as melting of ice above 0 °C, evaporation of water and dissolving NH₄Cl in water are spontaneous.

Entropy (S) is a measure of the degree of randomness or disorder of a system. For a substance, S(gas) > S(liquid) > S(solid). Entropy increases on melting, vaporisation, dissolving and when the number of gas molecules increases.
Entropy is a state function. For a reversible process at temperature T, ΔS = q_rev/T (units J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). The same heat causes a bigger entropy change at a lower temperature.
For a spontaneous process, the total entropy change is positive: ΔS_total = ΔS_system + ΔS_surroundings > 0. At equilibrium ΔS_total = 0.

example.q: Find the entropy change when 1 mol of ice melts at 273 K (Δ_fusH = 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹).
steps: Melting at the melting point is reversible: ΔS = q_rev/T.
ΔS = 22.01 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (positive: liquid is more disordered)

learn.reallife: A few drops of rose sharbat spread through a glass of water without stirring. Nothing pushes them; mixing simply increases entropy, which is why the process is spontaneous.

quiz.q: Which process is endothermic yet spontaneous at room temperature?

quiz.explain: NH₄Cl absorbs heat as it dissolves (the solution cools) but dissolves on its own because entropy increases.
quiz.mistake: Believes only exothermic changes can be spontaneous

quiz.q: Which has the highest entropy per mole at the same temperature?
quiz.explain: Gas molecules move freely and randomly, so the gas has the greatest disorder.
quiz.mistake: Thinks solids have higher entropy because they are 'stronger'

quiz.q: For which reaction does the entropy of the system decrease?
quiz.explain: 4 mol of gas become 2 mol of gas, so disorder falls.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the change in the number of gas molecules

quiz.q: A process has ΔS_system = −20 J K⁻¹ and ΔS_surroundings = +50 J K⁻¹. What is ΔS_total in J K⁻¹, and is it spontaneous?
quiz.explain: ΔS_total = −20 + 50 = +30 J K⁻¹ > 0, so the process is spontaneous even though the system's entropy falls.
quiz.mistake: Looks only at ΔS of the system

quiz.q: The same 1000 J of heat is transferred reversibly at 250 K and at 500 K. Which statement is correct?
options: The entropy change is the same
The entropy change is larger at 500 K
The entropy change is larger at 250 K (4 J K⁻¹) than at 500 K (2 J K⁻¹)
quiz.explain: ΔS = q/T: 1000/250 = 4 and 1000/500 = 2 J K⁻¹. Heat added to a colder system causes more disorder.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies q by T instead of dividing

quiz.q: What is the entropy change in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ when 1 mol of ice melts at 273 K (Δ_fusH = 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹)? Give two decimal places.
quiz.mistake: Uses kJ directly, getting 0.02

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Decrease in enthalpy alone cannot decide spontaneity. Reason (R): Some endothermic processes, such as evaporation of water, are spontaneous.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Endothermic spontaneous processes show that entropy also matters, so ΔH alone is not enough.
quiz.mistake: Thinks negative ΔH is always necessary for spontaneity

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If melting ice absorbs heat, why does it happen by itself? What is entropy?'
teach.praise: Superb! Entropy measures disorder; melting increases it, and if the total entropy of system plus surroundings rises, the process is spontaneous. Gappu's ice cream melts with a reason now!
teach.nudge: Good! What does entropy measure, and which total entropy change decides spontaneity?

topics.title: Gibbs energy and the temperature dependence of spontaneity

learn.hook: Limestone sits unchanged in a Rajasthan quarry for millions of years, yet in a lime kiln it breaks into quicklime. One equation, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, tells you the temperature at which it flips.
points: Gibbs energy G = H − TS (a state function, extensive). At constant temperature and pressure: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS (the Gibbs equation).
ΔG is the useful work obtainable from a process. Criterion at constant T and p: ΔG < 0 spontaneous; ΔG > 0 non-spontaneous (the reverse is spontaneous); ΔG = 0 equilibrium.
ΔH negative, ΔS positive: ΔG always negative, spontaneous at all temperatures. ΔH positive, ΔS negative: ΔG always positive, never spontaneous.
ΔH negative, ΔS negative: spontaneous only at low temperature (|TΔS| < |ΔH|). ΔH positive, ΔS positive: spontaneous only at high temperature (TΔS > ΔH).
The crossover temperature where ΔG = 0 is T = ΔH/ΔS. Above it (for ΔH > 0, ΔS > 0) the process becomes spontaneous. Convert ΔH to J (or ΔS to kJ) before dividing.

example.q: For a reaction, ΔH = +40 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +100 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Above what temperature is it spontaneous?
steps: At the crossover, ΔG = 0, so T = ΔH/ΔS.
T = 40 000 J mol⁻¹ ÷ 100 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
Above 400 K, TΔS > ΔH, so ΔG < 0.

learn.reallife: Lime kilns in Katni and Satna heat limestone above about 1100 K. Decomposing CaCO₃ is endothermic, but its entropy rises as CO₂ gas forms, so at high temperature ΔG turns negative.

games.title: Signs of ΔH and ΔS and spontaneity
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS (kJ mol⁻¹, with ΔS in kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)

quiz.q: For a reaction at 298 K, ΔH = −10 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = −50 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. What is ΔG in kJ mol⁻¹?
quiz.explain: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −10 − 298 × (−0.050) = −10 + 14.9 = +4.9 kJ mol⁻¹; non-spontaneous at 298 K.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert J to kJ or gets the sign of TΔS wrong

quiz.q: At what temperature (in K) does a reaction with ΔH = +179.1 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +160.2 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ reach ΔG = 0? Give the answer to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: T = ΔH/ΔS = 179 100/160.2 = 1117.98 K. Above this temperature, CaCO₃ decomposition becomes spontaneous.
quiz.mistake: Divides kJ by J without converting units

quiz.q: A reaction has ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0. It is:
quiz.explain: Both terms in ΔG = ΔH − TΔS are negative, so ΔG < 0 at every temperature.
quiz.mistake: Thinks temperature can make it non-spontaneous

quiz.q: A reaction with ΔH < 0 and ΔS < 0 is spontaneous:
quiz.explain: At low T, ΔH dominates and ΔG < 0; at high T, the positive −TΔS term wins and ΔG > 0.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the effect of temperature

quiz.q: What does ΔG = 0 indicate for a process at constant T and p?
quiz.explain: Neither direction is favoured; forward and reverse tendencies balance.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ΔG = 0 means no reaction can occur at all

quiz.q: For a reaction, ΔH = +40 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +100 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. What is ΔG at 300 K, in kJ mol⁻¹?
quiz.explain: ΔG = 40 − 300 × 0.100 = 40 − 30 = +10 kJ mol⁻¹, non-spontaneous at 300 K (it becomes spontaneous above 400 K).
quiz.mistake: Uses ΔS in J with ΔH in kJ

quiz.q: Which expression defines Gibbs energy?
quiz.explain: G = H − TS; at constant T this gives ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.
quiz.mistake: Confuses G with H = U + pV

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Decomposition of CaCO₃ is spontaneous only at high temperature. Reason (R): It is endothermic with a positive entropy change.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: For ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0, ΔG becomes negative only when TΔS exceeds ΔH, i.e. at high T.
quiz.mistake: Thinks endothermic reactions can never be spontaneous

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does Gibbs energy decide if a reaction will go, and why does temperature matter?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, negative means spontaneous, and temperature decides which term wins. Gappu can now predict the lime kiln!
teach.nudge: Close! What is the Gibbs equation, what sign of ΔG means spontaneous, and how can raising T change the result?

topics.title: Second and third laws; Gibbs energy and equilibrium constant

learn.hook: A reaction with ΔG° = −5.7 kJ mol⁻¹ at room temperature has K = 10; make it −57 kJ mol⁻¹ and K jumps to 10¹⁰. Small energy changes mean enormous changes in how far reactions go.
points: Second law of thermodynamics: the entropy of the universe (of an isolated system) increases in every spontaneous process; ΔS_total > 0.

Third law of thermodynamics: the entropy of a perfectly crystalline pure substance approaches zero as the temperature approaches absolute zero (0 K). This lets us calculate absolute entropies of substances, unlike enthalpies.
At equilibrium, Δ_rG = 0. For standard Gibbs energy, Δ_rG° = −RT ln K = −2.303 RT log K.
If Δ_rG° is negative, K > 1 (products favoured); if positive, K < 1 (reactants favoured); if Δ_rG° = 0, K = 1.
Rearranged: log K = −Δ_rG°/(2.303 RT). Use R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and Δ_rG° in J mol⁻¹. At 298 K, 2.303RT = 5705.85 J mol⁻¹.

example.q: Find Δ_rG° at 298 K for a reaction with K = 100 (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹).

learn.reallife: Indian fertiliser plants choose the temperature of ammonia synthesis using Δ_rG° = −RT ln K. At low temperature K is large but the reaction is slow, so engineers balance thermodynamics with speed.

games.title: Sign of Δ_rG° and value of K
Laws of thermodynamics: true or false?
items: The entropy of the universe increases in a spontaneous process
A perfect crystal at 0 K has zero entropy
Absolute entropies of substances cannot be calculated
The third law provides a zero point, so absolute entropies can be found.
A positive Δ_rG° means products are strongly favoured at equilibrium
Positive Δ_rG° gives K < 1, so reactants are favoured.
This links standard Gibbs energy to the equilibrium constant.

quiz.q: What is Δ_rG° in kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K for a reaction with K = 10 (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)? Give two decimal places.
quiz.mistake: Uses ln instead of 2.303 log without the factor, giving −2.48

quiz.q: A reaction at 298 K has Δ_rG° = −11.41 kJ mol⁻¹. What is log K (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Gets the sign wrong in the rearrangement

quiz.q: If Δ_rG° for a reaction is positive, then the equilibrium constant K is:
quiz.explain: −RT ln K > 0 means ln K < 0, so K < 1: reactants are favoured.
quiz.mistake: Thinks positive ΔG° means K > 1

quiz.q: Which statement is the third law of thermodynamics?
options: Energy of the universe is constant
Entropy of the universe always increases in spontaneous processes
Entropy of a perfectly crystalline substance approaches zero as T approaches 0 K
quiz.explain: The third law fixes a zero of entropy for perfect crystals at absolute zero.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the third law with the second law

quiz.q: The second law of thermodynamics can be stated as:
options: In a spontaneous process the entropy of the universe increases
Energy can neither be created nor destroyed
quiz.explain: ΔS_universe > 0 for spontaneous processes.
quiz.mistake: Gives the first law instead

quiz.q: At equilibrium, which is true?
quiz.explain: Δ_rG (not Δ_rG°) is zero at equilibrium; Δ_rG° is a fixed value related to K.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Δ_rG with Δ_rG°

quiz.q: A reaction has K = 1 at 298 K. What is its Δ_rG° in kJ mol⁻¹?
quiz.mistake: Uses log 1 = 1

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Reactions with large negative Δ_rG° go almost to completion. Reason (R): A large negative Δ_rG° corresponds to a very large equilibrium constant.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: K = 10^(−Δ_rG°/2.303RT); a large negative Δ_rG° makes K huge, so products dominate at equilibrium.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Δ_rG° says how fast the reaction goes

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What do the second and third laws say, and how is ΔG° connected to the equilibrium constant?'
teach.praise: Excellent! The second law says universal entropy rises, the third sets S = 0 for perfect crystals at 0 K, and Δ_rG° = −2.303RT log K links energy with equilibrium. Gappu has mastered thermodynamics!
teach.nudge: Nearly! State the second and third laws, and write the equation linking Δ_rG° and K.
